newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukrainian politicians lament deputy's killing.
newsitem.headline: Ukrainian politicians lament deputy's killing.

text.p: Ukraine's political world on Tuesday mourned a prominent parliamentarian who was mowed down in a gangland-style killing and security officials begged for more funding to break the former Soviet republic's crime wave.

"How did it happen that a people's deputy, father of three sons, was shot in broad daylight in an airport, an area of increased security, and his body was left lying on the tarmac for four hours?" Yevhen Marchuk, a leading liberal deputy, said.
"It is a political killing. It shows that Ukraine, despite the many steps it has made to reform, still has much to do in terms of democratisation," he told Reuters outside parliament.
Marchuk summed up the mood inside parliament to Sunday's killing of Yevhen Shcherban, his wife and one other person shortly after they stepped off a plane.
Three men dressed as policemen sprayed the group with dozens of bullets near the VIP section of Donetsk airport in eastern Ukraine, also wounding one of Shcherban's sons and three aides.
Shcherban was a well-known tycoon, owner of a trading company and linked to the lucrative world of energy and metals.
A big spray of flowers marked Shcherban's seat as parliament began a sombre session on crime with a minute's silence.
Ukraine has been the scene of a string of attacks blamed on in-fighting between "bandit" mafia groups, and people with links to them, which have emerged since independence in 1991.

"We are now in the process of privatisation and unfortunately a special type of businessman has been created...who in many cases cannot cut his links with the past," Security Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin told Reuters.
Security service head Volodymyr Radchenko also expressed concern that a new wave of sell-offs could spark further such attacks as people fought to grab a share of Ukraine's wealth.
Interior Minister Yuri Kravchenko complained of a lack of funds and equipment to the 230,000-strong police force.
"We should reduce our force by 140,000 men, judging by the funds we got this year...Who will protect Ukraine from crime?"
Ukraine's bloodiest violent incident was in 1995 when a bomb killed the head of a top soccer club and leading businessman and four bodyguards at the start of a match in Donetsk stadium.
Horbulin said security services had been badly prepared for the new Ukraine as it emerged from the Soviet era, when only the safety of senior Communist Party members was a consideration.

"We have only now started to focus our attention on the security of the individual. But what can be done when individuals in the past were never at the centre of attention unless they were members of the nomenklatura?" he said.
